**Question 1.** Which building characteristics best predict a building's GHG intensity?

This document uses the cleaned data from Part 1 (render `01_data_preparation_eda.Rmd` first). The Python
version is `python/02_q1_regression.ipynb`.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
# ---- Setup ----
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(rpart)
library(randomForest)

theme_set(theme_minimal())
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5)

bldg <- read.csv("../data/processed/buildings_latest_r.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
bldg$log_n_buildings <- log(bldg$n_buildings)
dim(bldg)
```

# 1. Approach

The approach mirrors the Python version: one row per building (latest report); target
`log(GHG intensity)`; features available without energy bills (property group, log10 floor area,
building age, log number of buildings, distance to downtown, latitude, data year); numeric features
standardized with training-set means and standard deviations; models compared against a
property-group-only baseline:

- linear regression (property group as a factor; its first level, Grocery, is the reference);
- a regression tree (maximum depth 5, at least 30 buildings per leaf);
- a random forest (400 trees, at least 5 buildings per leaf, 4 of the 7 features tried at each split).

The data are split 80/20 within each property group, and 5-fold cross-validation is run on the training
set.

```{r split}
num_cols <- c("log_floor_area", "building_age", "log_n_buildings", "dist_downtown_km", "lat", "year")
data <- bldg[, c(num_cols, "property_group", "log_ghg_intensity")]
data$property_group <- factor(data$property_group)

# Stratified 80/20 split by property group
set.seed(42)
idx_train <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(data)), data$property_group),
                           function(i) sample(i, round(0.8 * length(i)))))
train <- data[idx_train, ]
test <- data[-idx_train, ]

# Standardize numeric features with training-set statistics
mu <- sapply(train[num_cols], mean)
sdv <- sapply(train[num_cols], sd)
train[num_cols] <- sweep(sweep(train[num_cols], 2, mu), 2, sdv, "/")
test[num_cols] <- sweep(sweep(test[num_cols], 2, mu), 2, sdv, "/")
cat("Training:", nrow(train), "buildings   Test:", nrow(test), "buildings\n")
```

# 2. Training and evaluation

```{r models}
fit_model <- function(name, tr) {
  switch(name,
    "Property group only" = lm(log_ghg_intensity ~ property_group, data = tr),
    "Linear regression" = lm(log_ghg_intensity ~ ., data = tr),
    "Regression tree" = rpart(log_ghg_intensity ~ ., data = tr, method = "anova",
                              control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 5, minbucket = 30, cp = 0)),
    "Random forest" = randomForest(log_ghg_intensity ~ ., data = tr, ntree = 400, nodesize = 5,
                                   mtry = 4))
}
r2 <- function(y, p) 1 - sum((y - p)^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2)
model_names <- c("Property group only", "Linear regression", "Regression tree", "Random forest")

# 5-fold cross-validated R-squared on the training set
set.seed(42)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(train)))
cv_r2 <- sapply(model_names, function(m) sapply(1:5, function(k) {
  fit <- fit_model(m, train[folds != k, ])
  r2(train$log_ghg_intensity[folds == k], predict(fit, train[folds == k, ]))
}))

set.seed(42)
fits <- lapply(setNames(model_names, model_names), fit_model, tr = train)
preds <- lapply(fits, predict, newdata = test)
y <- test$log_ghg_intensity

results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(model_names, function(m) {
  p <- preds[[m]]
  data.frame(model = m,
             cv_r2 = sprintf("%.3f +/- %.3f", mean(cv_r2[, m]), sd(cv_r2[, m])),
             test_r2 = round(r2(y, p), 3),
             test_rmse_log = round(sqrt(mean((y - p)^2)), 3),
             test_mae_kg = round(mean(abs(exp(y) - exp(p))), 3),
             median_abs_error_kg = round(median(abs(exp(y) - exp(p))), 3))
}))
results
```

```{r pred-actual, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
ggplot(data.frame(actual = exp(y), predicted = exp(preds[["Random forest"]])),
       aes(actual, predicted)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "steelblue", size = 1) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Random Forest: Predicted vs Actual (test set)",
       x = "Actual GHG intensity (kg CO2e/sq ft, log scale)",
       y = "Predicted GHG intensity (kg CO2e/sq ft, log scale)")
```

**Interpretation.** The random forest explains `r results$test_r2[4]` of the variance in log GHG
intensity on the test set and linear regression `r results$test_r2[2]`, while property group alone
explains `r results$test_r2[1]`; the regression tree reaches `r results$test_r2[3]`. As in Python,
building characteristics predict GHG intensity only weakly, and nearly all of what they do predict comes
from property type.

# 3. Which characteristics matter?

```{r permutation}
# Drop in test R-squared when one feature is shuffled (10 repeats)
rf <- fits[["Random forest"]]
base <- r2(y, preds[["Random forest"]])
features <- c(num_cols, "property_group")
set.seed(42)
drops <- sapply(features, function(f) mean(replicate(10, {
  shuffled <- test
  shuffled[[f]] <- sample(shuffled[[f]])
  base - r2(y, predict(rf, shuffled))
})))
imp <- data.frame(feature = features, mean_r2_drop = round(drops, 4)) %>% arrange(desc(mean_r2_drop))

ggplot(imp, aes(x = reorder(feature, mean_r2_drop), y = mean_r2_drop)) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen") + coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Random Forest: Permutation Importance (test set)", x = "Feature",
       y = "Drop in test R-squared when the feature is shuffled")
imp
```

```{r coefficients}
coefs <- coef(fits[["Linear regression"]])[-1]
data.frame(term = names(coefs), coefficient = round(coefs, 3),
           pct_change_in_ghg = round((exp(coefs) - 1) * 100, 1), row.names = NULL) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(coefficient)))
```

```{r save}
write.csv(results, "../report/figures/q1_results_r.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(imp, "../report/figures/q1_permutation_importance_r.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

# 4. Discussion

The R models agree with the Python ones. **Property group** is by far the most important feature
(shuffling it lowers the forest's R-squared by `r imp$mean_r2_drop[imp$feature == "property_group"]`),
followed by **building age** (`r imp$mean_r2_drop[imp$feature == "building_age"]`); floor area, location
and year matter little. In the linear model, multifamily buildings emit
`r round((1 - exp(coefs["property_groupMultifamily"])) * 100)`% less per sq ft than grocery stores.

The exact numbers differ slightly from Python because the train/test split is drawn by R's random number
generator and the forest implementations differ. The conclusion is the same: a building's type sets the
expected range of its emissions, but where it falls in that range depends on equipment and operation,
which these characteristics do not capture.
